name: Femi Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a blast hole drill at an iron ore mine, the open-cut kind. I set up on the pattern the surveyors mark out, drill the holes to depth, and the shot crew loads them later. I'm still on the learner's side, about two and a half years, after fourteen years delivering beer for a brewery until they shut the regional depot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a good day on the drill, and a bad one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when the ground's even, the bit doesn't jam and I finish my pattern before crib. A bad day is when I drift off the mark and Gary, the drill supervisor, makes me redo a row while everyone watches. I'm not fast, but I'm careful, and I like that nobody's on a computer up there except the drill's own screen, which I keep as simple as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the easy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. Maybe something like, see, all that fuss for nothing, at the crib table. I don't really post online, Claire does the family stuff on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a weight off. I'd get to stay on the drill, get better, maybe get my pay up a level next year. That's the life I signed up for when I left the brewery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, drill my patterns, do the extra training hours Gary keeps telling me to do. We'd keep the four months we've saved and maybe finally fix the back fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting home and everything's where you left it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you keep the drill's screen simple. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are all these menus on it, auto-levelling and so on. The young guys use all of it. I use the bits I know and leave the rest, because if I press something I don't understand, I end up with a crooked hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Theo's thirteen and wants a gaming computer, so we'd argue about that. Nina's ten and she'd just want to know if we're still going to her aunt's at Christmas.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe something like 'all that fuss for nothing' at the crib table. I don't post online; my partner handles that.
S0.think: It'd be a weight off: I'd stay on the drill, get better and maybe move up a pay level next year. That's the life I signed up for after the brewery.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and drilling his patterns, and does the extra training hours his supervisor recommends. Keeps the four months of savings and fixes the back fence.
S0.feel: Calm, like getting home and finding everything where he left it.
S0.quote: If I press something I don't understand, I end up with a crooked hole.
S0.fieldNote: Femi's resistance to technology is quiet and practical rather than angry: he uses the parts of the drill's screen he trusts and ignores the rest. He's pragmatic, not political. His wants are simple: steady pay, the fence, Christmas at his sister-in-law's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one could be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will do what pays, and we'll see how it shakes out. I'm not one to march about it. But I'd say they owe it to people to be straight about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it'd be a while before it got to me. Our drills are old, and the company's tight with money. But I know some sites already run drills from a room, so maybe I'm kidding myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep my head down, and see what the company announces. If they offered a course, I'd probably do it, but I wouldn't go looking. We'd stop the extra spending, like the gaming computer for Theo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like a noise in the drill rig you keep hoping is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe you're kidding yourself. Which part do you believe more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, depending on the day. On a good shift I think, nah, these old rigs will be here till I retire. On a bad shift I think they'd be glad of an excuse to get rid of the slow guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Theo about the computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not this year, mate. He'd sulk for a week. I wouldn't tell him why, I don't want him worrying about my job at thirteen.

S1.say: I'd say it's business, companies do what pays, and we'll see how it shakes out. They owe people honesty, but I won't march about it.
S1.think: I think it'd take a while to reach me because our drills are old and the company is tight with money. But some sites already run drills from a room, so maybe I'm kidding myself.
S1.do: Keeps drilling with his head down and waits to see what the company announces. Would take a course if offered but won't seek one, and cancels the gaming computer for his son.
S1.feel: Uneasy, hoping a worrying noise is nothing.
S1.quote: They'd be glad of an excuse to get rid of the slow guy.
S1.fieldNote: Femi sees change through the lens of business sense, not blame. He openly swings between denial and fear depending on how his shift went. He shields his son from the reason for the cutback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Geez.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better have something ready, because people won't sit quietly if a whole town loses its jobs. I'm not left or right on it, it's just common sense. You can't put a mortgage on hold with a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in real trouble. I'm not good with new tech, I'm junior, and two years is nothing. I left one job that vanished already, and I don't know what's left for a guy like me if the drills and the trucks both go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd cut everything back and keep every dollar of our four months. I'd talk to my brother-in-law, who runs a fencing business, about working for him, because people will still want fences built by someone they know, at least for a while. I'd sit tight at the mine as long as they'll keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's falling away under the rig. I'd be awake at three in the morning, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd freeze, that's the honest truth. I'm slow with new things in the best of times. I'd still be thinking about what to do when it was already done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Claire say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire would make a list, that's what she does. She'd sit me down with a budget on paper and tell me which bills we can push. She's the one who'd keep us steady.

S2.say: I'd say the government had better have something ready, because towns won't sit quietly if everyone loses their jobs. It's common sense, not left or right.
S2.think: I think I'd be in real trouble: junior, not good with tech, and two years is nothing. I've already lost one job that vanished, and I don't know what's left for me.
S2.do: Cuts spending back and protects the four months of savings. Talks to his brother-in-law about fencing work while staying at the mine as long as they'll keep him.
S2.feel: Like the ground falling away under the rig, awake at three in the morning.
S2.quote: With two years I'd freeze, that's the honest truth.
S2.fieldNote: Femi is honest that his first response to fast change would be to freeze. His fallback is family: his partner's budgeting and his brother-in-law's fencing business. He frames his demands as common sense rather than politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly if everyone stops arguing and plans. Companies, government, everyone. I'd say that to the guys at work, who'd mostly agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years helps a little. Theo would be finishing school and Nina would be in high school. But I'm not the type to start over at forty-five, so I'd probably hang on too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling, save harder to get us to six months, and I'd start doing weekends with my brother-in-law on the fencing, just to see if I like it. If the mine started cutting, I'd move over to him full-time. I wouldn't do a course unless the company made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the two-year one. I'd have a back door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably hang on too long. What would make you go sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire telling me to. Or seeing Gary leave, because if the supervisor goes, the rest of us aren't far behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fencing's hands-on work too. Robots could reach it in this picture. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know. But a farmer wanting a fence on a hill, with rocks everywhere, he's going to call a bloke he knows. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's a slower bet than the mine.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to do this properly if companies and government stop arguing and plan. Most of the guys at work would agree with that.
S3.think: I think five years helps a little with the kids further along, but I'm not the type to start over at forty-five, so I'd probably hang on too long.
S3.do: Keeps drilling, saves toward six months and starts weekend fencing work with his brother-in-law to test it. Moves to fencing full-time if the mine starts cutting, and avoids courses unless required.
S3.feel: Anxious but less so, with a back door available.
S3.quote: A farmer wanting a fence on a hill, with rocks everywhere, he's going to call a bloke he knows.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Femi a back door, and he builds it through family rather than training. He knows he'll hang on too long and names his partner and supervisor as the signals that would move him. He accepts the challenge about fencing but holds to his reasoning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses later. Everyone should have a plan B by then, me included. Not much more to it than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage would be under half, the kids would be grown. I'd ride the drill as long as I could and then go to fencing. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the drill for the next few years, keep saving, and pay a bit extra off the mortgage. Around year five I'd start building up the fencing work on weekends. I'd wait and watch what the mine does with its drills first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but nothing I can't sleep on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AGI arrives in 2036 and the fencing slows too, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm fifty-three with no trade and no tech skills, I know. I'd hope by then the government's sorted something. I don't love hoping, but there it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young guys with big loans on their utes. They spend like the money's forever. I was the same at the brewery when I was their age.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no one has an excuse later; everyone needs a plan B, me included.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three, with the mortgage under half and the kids grown, it feels manageable to ride the drill and then go to fencing.
S4.do: Keeps working the drill for several years while saving and paying extra off the mortgage. Builds weekend fencing work around year five, after watching what the mine does with its drills.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but not enough to lose sleep.
S4.quote: I don't love hoping, but there it is.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Femi's plan is simply a slower version of the five-year one. He admits the gap in it and rests on hope, which he doesn't like. He worries about younger colleagues spending like he once did.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd freeze. What would help is someone just telling us clearly, at the mine, what's coming and when. And some money to tide families over while blokes like me work out the next thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how embarrassing it is to be the learner at forty-three. Twenty-year-olds explain things to me. If I lost this job too, I'm not sure I'd have it in me to be the new guy a third time.

headlineQuote: I'm not sure I'd have it in me to be the new guy a third time.
portrait: Femi Moreau is 43 and runs a blast hole drill at an open-cut iron ore mine, two and a half years in after the brewery he delivered for closed its depot. He's practical and in the middle politically, sees AI as business doing what pays, and avoids technology he doesn't understand. He's calm on the plateau, swings between hope and doubt in Steady Disruption, and admits he'd freeze if AGI came in two years. With more time, he builds a back door through his brother-in-law's fencing business rather than retraining.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he knows he would freeze rather than act.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, honest notice from the mine about what's coming and when, and money to tide families over while people find the next thing.
